Sorry all you Ronald Reagan fans, but his policies and actions—however well-intentioned—directly or indirectly—led to the horrors described in this article:    I.e., state institutions downsizing or closing, federal, community grant funding getting slashed, and the local emergency room becoming the de facto, 24/7 nexus of the nation's psychiatric crisis. Nurses and other hospital staff have been under siege ever since.

It was a classic tale of unintended consequences. The structural impacts of Reagan's executive and legislative decisions while he was Governor of California and then President, profoundly accelerated the deinstitutionalization movement already underway.  His legislative actions stripped federal oversight and reduced public funding for existing psychiatric institutions. The community-based care network meant to replace those facilities was severely underfunded and/or left unbuilt.

Thousands of discharged individuals with severe conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder ended up on the streets without medication or support networks.Jails and state prisons became the nation's default mental institutions. These, in turn, became revolving doors, leading right back to our streets hospitals. It is hard to picture a solution emerging any time soon, with our system of government collapsing before our eyes.

Students know their strengths and generally where they belong; they should be supported in finding the appropriate placements (which actually happened, more or less, when my kids were going through it back then). Moreover, France is a member of NATO and the EU, both of which are suddenly trying desperately to increase their military budgets, and commitments. 

Military alliances should be a means, by virtue of common purposes, of reducing each member nation's overall defense expenditures, and not to increase them.

In addition, France, whether inside NATO or as in recent decades outside of NATO, is a nuclear power.  It shouldn't try, given its small size, to be both a major nuclear power and have a powerful regular traditional military force.  

One of the other, or both simultaneously, should be reduced, or its military alliances, should recoup part of its expenses in being both, particularly if both its nuclear and non nuclear forces are keys to its alliances.

Such drawdowns could more immediately help to provide economic assistance to France during this time of political stress.  

In any event, this should not be a time when France is trying to make the EU into a military power in its own right by requiring members to bear the cost of creating the EU's military force.

Those who stake out a categorical opposition to all forms of Zionism, including cultural Zionism, on the grounds that such commitments are incompatible with pluralistic democracy assume a considerable burden of consistency.

They must explain why the same principle does not entail an equally sweeping repudiation of other states that privilege particular national, cultural, or religious identities.

What of the Islamic Republic of Iran? The Gulf monarchies? Or even England, with its established state church, the Church of England?

These are not equivalent political systems, nor do their particular histories absolve Israel of criticism. But objections to particular Israeli policies cannot justify the categorical repudiation of Zionism, including its cultural expressions. Such a sweeping condemnation demands an equally universal principle.

In the absence of a consistent answer, such high-minded universalism rings hollow, and the charge of an antisemitic double standard acquires greater warrant.

I am continuously amazed to read comments about how our social model is unsustainable, how our economy supposedly still is stuck in the 19th century and how Macron failed to reform enough.

Macron passed dozens of reforms since 2015, which have come after dozens of reforms passed since Mitterrand in the 1980s, all with the same objectives: liberalization of markets of all kinds, lessening of social welfare programmes, tax hikes on the wealthy and on capital gains ;
and similar results: increased poverty, growing unemployment, stagnating corporate investment, no meaningful help to small enterprises, and insufficient investment into essential infrastructure (hospitals, schools, energy networks…), all ending up in increased inequalities.

The same recipe has been applied in most Western countries: no wonder anti system parties are thriving !
Fellow readers, have you ever opened a book on the history of economic systems and studied anything that is not Hayek-derived liberalism ? You will learn that one of the staples of stable economies post-war has been welfare, which allows people to afford the ups and downs of life, opens up perspectives for those not born wealthy, and that public investment is one of the main drivers of economic expansion (the Keynesian multiplicator).

It is not “mathematical” that countries are doomed to reduce welfare systems. That is liberal brainwash: our economies have never been larger !
It is a question of how this wealth is shared, whom it benefits.

Policy aside, I think the characters of Macron and Le Pen together represent the French political id perfectly. The centrist coalition versus the fringe right. Jupiter versus The Pen. Whoever is in power, you can bet in a few years the streets of Paris will be smoking again. And again, and again...

comments.name: OTB
comments.body: I thought Katrin Benhold’s article would explain why Macron and his 2017 promises to unite France and boost the economy have failed. In France, total social security contributions range from 45 to 68 percent of salary, with up to 23 percent paid by the employee and up to 45 percent by the employer. The French can retire at age 63. This is an economic burden that every French citizen must bear. In 2017, Macron promised to change this, and when he set out to implement his reform program, he encountered fierce resistance from the “Yellow Vests” movement, which also supported the current protests. The protests in 2018 prompted Macron to reduce and even abandon his reform plans and, combined with lower corporate and income taxes, increased France’s enormous budget deficit—which now is so high that no French government has the financial leeway to invest in anything other than repaying its debts.

comments.name: John David Forsgren
comments.body: Ms. Dowd, thank you for your thoughtful article. But a comment or two... As someone who doesn't/didn't live in a "major" American city, Portland, Oregon, I've read article after article after article talking about the impact of AIDS on NYC, LA or San Francisco. I don't doubt the impact on those cities. I know the impact AIDS had on those cities. In 1989, I sat down with a best friend, and we wrote down the names of the men we'd known who had died. When we got to 100, we looked at each other, and put our pens down, and wept. In the early 1980's, I remember getting a slightly panicked call from my father who practiced medicine in one of the small towns in southern Oregon. He wanted me to connect him with a physician friend of mine in Portland who had many AIDS patients. Young men were showing up in my Dad's waiting room after having driven sometimes hundreds of miles to see him. The doctors in their communities refused to see them. They knew my father would, so they sent them to my dad. And he did, with the very few treatment options that existed. Nothing, he said, had embarrassed him more than his profession's response to these young men. AIDS was affecting and killing young men in big cities, small cities, and small towns. Even in the early 80's. AIDS was everywhere, and devastating families and communities everywhere.

As workers were laid off I was assigned to maintain a system that monitors several environmental air samples that detect arsine, among other gasses nicknamed "sniff and drop deads". Arsine contains arsenic. Another contains cyanide. There were many.

You could smell the arsine in the air and the monitoring system showed levels well above the alarm limits but the evacuation alarms had been disconnected. Workers told me they had complained but nothing was done about it so they quit complaining to stay out of trouble and kept working to pay the bills. I refused to work in the area and should have called OSHA.

In another instance workers were required to to carefully walk atop a 7 ft tall narrow concrete dividing wall in a secondary containment pit for tanks containing  hazardous chemicals. No catwalk no guard rails. A fall to the left you you're soaked in a foot of 50% sodium hydroxide that had leaked out of the tank. Fall to the right and you're enveloped in hydrochloric acid fumes spewing out if it's tank. If you got to the chemical pumps you couldn't stand on the rotted out plywood "temporary" decking so you stood on the frame inhaling acid fumes. I was able to resolve that nightmare and coworkers couldn't thank me enough. 

Nut management couldn't have cared less. Not their problem and fixing them cost $$ which did affect their bonuses.

The title is an interesting choice of words.

Until now, India had no functioning democracy at all, as the media narrative goes. The largest voter mobilization in human history, the independence of the Election Commission, etc., did little to alter the narrative that Indian democracy is never really a democracy.

All of a sudden, a protest changes everything. Now India has a democracy, and it is working!

I lived in India for 30 years and participated in several street protests over reservations and other grievances.

I can guarantee you that protests rarely happen without forces behind them. During my student days, I was approached by various groups to do this or that, as I was a student representative.

comments.name: Anna

There is a lot of frustration in these comments about inequality. I too want billionaires to pay their fair share of taxes. But, insomuch as these wealthy individuals are not actively cheating our tax codes, "they should pay taxes instead of doing philanthropy" is a false dichotomy. And so is "governments should be responsible for this work, not the wealthy!"

The reality is, if you are in the United States or another high income country, *you* are probably part of the *global* 10%. Perhaps even the global 1%. That's inequality that should make you very uncomfortable indeed.

Effective altruists focused on global health recognize that money can save lives. By Givewell's math it takes (conservatively) $5,000 in charitable giving to literally save a life, if donated to an effective charity. 

Laugh about EA's focus on randomized control trials and metrics (I know we can be an odd bunch). But EA philanthropists aren't building theaters with their names on the wall. They want to save lives. And if you are truly giving money because you want to save lives, it actually does matter if the organization works. It actually does matter if giving $20,000 to an organization saves 4 lives or 1.

Thank you for guiding me to books I probably wouldn't have read and reading them with a critical eye. What alarms me is the trend to substitute AI analysis for literary criticism.   Whether you agree with Fiedler or not, his distinct view focuses a lens for interpreting and comparing American literature to world literature. You can reject or accept, but you bring your own critical opinion. AI can provide an adequate plot summary; mostly, it misses the Disappearers. It helped guide me on what to expect in Absalom. Contemporary stage magic and mentalism often leave audiences immersed in a state of uncritical wonder, encouraging a retreat into pseudo-scientific belief and suspension of critical thought. This marks a stark departure from the traditions of Harry Houdini and James Randi. Both men understood that the greatest service a magician can perform is not to convince the public of miracles, but to expose the mechanisms of deception—reminding us that what looks like supernatural mind-reading or levitation is merely clever sleight of hand and psychological trickery.

Yet, there remains a deeper, unsettling paradox at play. If we were to judge reality solely by the evidence presented on stage, the flawless execution of an illusion can make scientific laws appear secondary—as though physics and biology are merely light suggestions easily overridden by a practitioner. In an era where misdirection is no longer confined to the stage but increasingly shapes public discourse and digital media, the legacy of Houdini and Randi is a crucial reminder: extraordinary claims demand rigorous scrutiny, and the appearance of a phenomenon should never be mistaken for its proof.

This is a classic case of facially-neutral proxies to engineer the demographic balance of an admitted class. Time to put a stop to this. 

The article and the comments lacked context, so I dug in a bit. The case is Association for Education Fairness (AFEF) v. Montgomery County Board of Education, involving Montgomery County Public Schools (MCPS). 

With the adjustment for local norms, a student in the lowest poverty tier school had to score 60th percentile on the national scale in math and a student from the most affluent schools 93-94th percentile to be placed in the lottery. Dozens of students with scores of 98th and 99th percentile did not get in whereas those with scores in the 60s got in. 

To note: Scores were NOT adjusted for individual student demographics; just the school demographics. So, if you came from a poor family but went to an affluent school, you were out of luck. 

The implementation of local norming and lottery-based admissions sharply reduced the representation of Asian American students while substantially increasing seats for Black and Hispanic students. Prior to the reforms, Asian American students held between 45% and 64% of magnet enrollments and following the policy, this went to 18% to 31%. 

For all practical purposes, this is racial favoritism/discrimination.  You shouldn't be able to do this by using proxies. Not even sure the unprepared students benefit from going to a magnet school (but the prepared ones who didn't get in surely lose).

In 1968, I was born, and subsequently raised, in Los Angeles.  By the time I was 13 years of age, I began to fear death. By 1985, when testing occurred with anonymity, I had my first HTLV-III--not yet called HIV--test.  During the 2-week wait for my results, the act of sex became fused with the reality of death.  During this 2-weeks, I determined the best method for suicide when disease symptoms emerged.  I think it was the fear that I lived with, daily, that inspired my AIDS education work and time with ActUP-LA and other activist groups.

Now, I am an almost-58-year-old transwoman and it seems to be almost random luck that I am HIV-negative.  To this day my brain struggles to reconcile the AIDS pandemic.  I recall vividly the political and public health fiascos--then and now, the survivor's guilt, and the memories of beauty, love, and loss... and fear... This article captivated me.  Thank you for the gift of memories and moments to ponder.  I am now a little closer to that elusive reconciliation.

I lost my best friend 34 years ago to AIDS. His friendship prior to his disease and its progression was marked with travel and conversation. Both of growing up in the suburbs in the 50s 60s and 70s. We met at work and rest was history. 
Nothing prepared me for this virus and his journey. And in the end we forgave each other for whatever if there ever was a transgression. In his end I found I was more mature and wise than I ever knew. Life for me changed and has in many ways propelled me to think and feel differently about life. 
Aging is a gift that not many men and yes women and children did not have the chance to experience. And our friendship and my friend’s legacy is what I carry forward every day , every year.

Imagine Renaissance Florence, where fragrance was more than indulgence it was an invisible shield, a source of joy, comfort and personal power. Perhaps Catherine de’ Medici understood the influence of scent centuries before modern aromachology began exploring its connection to emotion, memory and our state of mind.

My studies in archaeology at UC San Diego, ancient incense trade routes, and the relationship of fragrance, civilization and human consciousness. Recently, I presented at a Newport Beach conference on the higher ages and the Yugas, exploring connections between ancient wisdom and our evolving understanding of consciousness and scent. 

At my Encinitas fragrance studio, CardiffScents, in Cardiff by the Sea, California, I explore this very relationship. My fragrances Dispeller of Darkness, with beeswax, patchouli, citrus and sandalwood, and Breeze of Bliss, with rose, citrus and patchouli, are conceived as invisible force fields of scent, creating aromatic atmospheres that accompany the wearer through the day.

Much as Catherine surrounded herself with fragrance, we can think of perfume as more than an adornment. It becomes an invisible landscape we carry with us, where ancient wisdom, modern science and the art of perfumery meet.

Through CardiffScents, I hope to illuminate the deeper possibilities of aromachology: fragrance not merely as something beautiful to wear, but as an invisible force that shapes how we feel, remember and experience the world.

comments.body: The article argues that phones should be banned at concerts because they distract people from enjoying the music. It highlights Phoebe Bridgers decision to ban phones on her tour so fans can focus more on the performance. The article suggests that phones can block other people’s views and take away from the experience. I agree that phones should be banned at concerts because people spend money to see their favorite artists, and they should enjoy the moment instead of recording everything. Banning phones would help fans focus on the music and make better memories.

comments.name: Eloise
comments.body: I’m in full support of Phoebe Bridgers decision to “ban” phones at her concert. As someone who didn’t go to her concert when she came in my city- but have friends who went- I can just tell how special it was for them. It’s so interesting to see people talk about it online as well, it makes it feel like they’re in their own community with something they can all relate to, and no one from the outside can have an input. It’s something really special that opened my eyes as someone who takes about 100 pictures and videos whenever I go to a concert. I love capturing the memories, and taking pictures with friends, but there’s something even more special about a mental image instead of a physical one. It definitely can make people more tuned into the concert in general, instead of checking notifications or getting distracted by something other than what’s in front of you. I’d say that it’s a very interesting concept, but I’d love to see more artists do it in the future.

This would allow everyone to capture meaningful moments without taking away from the live experience.

> While a blanket ban on all concerts might not work for every genre, soft policies or phone-free zones would greatly improve the overall experience. The only thing we really lose is a digital souvenir, but in return, we gain a far more memorable and shared live atmosphere.

At concerts, many people spend more time recording videos and taking pictures than actually watching the artist perform. Sometimes people are so focused on getting the perfect video that they miss the experience happening right in front of them. Without these devices, fans could pay more attention to the music, sing along, and connect with the artist and the people around them. I also think banning technology could make concerts feel more special and personal. Instead of looking at a screen, people would be able to look around, enjoy the atmosphere, and create memories they can remember without needing to record everything. Although I understand why some people would disagree with this decision, because they want to take pictures and videos to remember their favorite songs, I think being fully present can be more meaningful than having a video on your phone. Overall, I support her decision because concerts should be about enjoying live music and making memories, not just capturing content to post online

comments.name: Winston
comments.body: There is earlier, similar research on the antigen HLA-B27. B27, which is strongly correlated with ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, the inflammatory bowel diseases, reactive arthritis, juvenile arthritis, and uveitis, is more prevalent in the genomes of populations in northern cold climates, e.g., Inuits. And it is protective against many viruses, including HIV, flu, and Epstein-Barr. (Carriers of HLA-B27 are coined "long-term non-progressors" in the HIV world, I think.) The theory goes that an epidemic, likely flu, in Inuit populations in the distant past wiped out everyone who didn't carry HLA-B27.

Such as the male ability to not know when we are slightly cut or scratched until we see blood on the floor. Then we have to search our own bodies to find the cut. Not an uncommon male trait. I learned it was a leftover trait from our ancient hunter past, when we were chasing game (with spears) through brambles and such. The small cuts were unavoidable and ignored. It's a trait we still have. Another is the male sex drive topping out around age 17, and into our early 20's. Reason: In ancient times males simply didn't live that long. Making it to age 30 was quite an accomplishment, given our hunter lifestyle and the dangers of hunts and war with other groups or tribes. Nature compensated for our short lifespan in the reproductive cycle. Women, on the other hand, stayed mostly in shelters, and avoided the male risks. They naturally lived longer, were captured and not killed in wars. Their sex drive increases in their 30's as a natural result. 
   There is much from our ancient past we still carry. Being only 5000 years away from that time isn't all that much in evolutionary terms. So, it's no surprise what once helped us, now hurts us. Nature hasn't had time to adapt us yet to our current living conditions. We need another 10,000 years.

Yet, she has the strength to express her disagreement with her parents very publicly, all the while knowing that they would likely be subjected to withering criticism.  This is a young woman who has real strength of character.  She and her parents should be celebrated, not criticized or maligned.  Furthermore, Ms. Hannah-Jones identified the real tragedy here is that she and her husband were forced to make this decision at all . . . . that is a failure of the NYC public schools, not their failure.  While there is no simple answer, as Ms. Hannah-Jones acknowledges, it starts with public officials and the public as a whole acknowledging that a solution requires a sustained, long-term commitment that focuses intensely on the needs of public students themselves both individually and collectively with all parties and interest groups sacrificing their individual self-interest for the benefit of the students.

HNJ is a deep thinking Journalist. Always has been so. She used her personal experience in this piece because that is her foundational look at NYC School Education experience from a perspective of a participant rather than an Interviewer. Nothing wrong with talking from personal experience and plumbing the depths of an issue from this approach. We as a thinking Society ask so much of what we want to see change and stand on opposite sides of what we believe is just and fair. We often see what we know is wrong but are unable to right the situation. Since we ask so much for people to think and then change and we watch changes affect how we live, why do Journalists have to live by certain Journalistic rules that may never change things but only show "sides" of issues. What HNJ writes is often thought provoking and true but yet, difficult to square in the Public Square. One part of her piece stated that School Choice added to inequality and she is, of course, 100 percent correct but those that are able to "choose" without having to make real choice always win. School Choice simply means more segregation between the haves and have nots. Why? This approach has always destroyed us as a Society and continues to do so. Phage therapy has been an idea over 100 years old.  Today, it is recognized that the proteins on the bacterial cell surface that the phage uses as receptors can readily generate mutants in the receptors under the selective pressure of the onslaught of phage, leading to lack of binding by the phage.  This had resulted in the use of mixtures of phages (cocktails) to mitigate resistance development to any one phage.   Also we have learned that bacteria have immune systems that can deal with some phage DNA once it enters the bacterial cell in CRISPR-Cas, which destroys the incoming DNA by cutting it.  CRISPR-CAs is employed for genetic engineering in other contexts in gene research

Another issue in phage therapy is that the phage, which are DNA or RNA are in protective coats made up of multiple proteins.   The immune system can respond to these foreign proteins and generate an immune response to the phage over time.  

So an interesting development in utilizing AI, but probably not addressing some of the other hurdles involved.

I was fortunate to see the opera yesterday evening in the company of my harp teacher who loves Missy Mazzoli's work. I was not familiar with it.

Met Opera missed the mark badly with so many of the new operas it staged over the past two or three seasons, including Grounded (Music by Jeanine Tesori and libretto by George Brant) which opened the 2024-2025 season and which I mention because Joshua Barone's review alludes to it.

But not last night. 

The entire production of Lincoln in the Bardo was glorious. Theatre at its best, opera at its best. Lincoln in the Bardo was simultaneously other worldly and believable. I was astonished when the interval arrived (the first act was a full 90 minutes). 

I found it mesmeric from beginning to end; Shakespeare, Scarlatti, and Sterne met Beckett, Saunders, Mazzoli and Vavrek

I was waiting for this review and while it does not disappoint, Joshua Barone has ruined the final moment for anyone who has not yet seen the production. Sometimes, less is more. It's one reason I rarely read reviews before going to see a production or concert.

When Branden Jacobs-Jenkins' Gloria was staged, critics were specifically asked not to write about a certain moment and audiences by inference were expected to allow others to experience the unexpected, first hand. I participated as a volunteer passenger/victim in one of these accident response simulations at my local airport.

The preparation for the simulation was extensive: volunteers were given a description of their injuries, inc. post-accident mental status. We were then shepherded to make-up were skilled makeup artists attempted to create realistic injuries, from minor contusions and abrasions to major burns.

A partial fuselage used for the simulations sitting near the edge of the airfield, and some sort of accelerant was ignited resulting in volumes of dark smoke. 

We volunteer passengers were instructed to go out anywhere on the airfield & adjacent we chose, from the tarmac and beyond. We could stand, lay down, wander aimlessly, scream, yell, or be totally silent; our choice.

The simulation began as the First responders came to the location where they conducted field triage using large colored tarps (I believe I recall green, yellow, red, and black; I was triaged to red based on my injuries and subsequently backboarded to a nearby ambulance. 

The two local hospitals had been alerted to the 'disaster' but the simulation ended before they actually transported me. 

I'm unable to speak to how realistic or effective the simulation was for the first responders; I only recall forgetting to remove my makeup as I subsequently went grocery shopping... and got some weird looks.

comments.name: Former officer, air defense

Many countries use jets for high altitude air defence. Only difference now is that the invaders are jet drones, not manned aircraft. That's an advantage as they (for now) don't fight back.

A proven and much published fact is that the ground-to-air missiles usually used to target high altitude drones are more than 10 times as expensive than then drone itself. A jet drone is estimated to cost $60,000. Missiles between $200,000 and $1m. 

Jets can (1) bring down larger numbers of drones in a single mission (2) do it relatively inexpensively. Article quote "one F-16 pilot recently shot down 10 jet-powered drones during a single flight"  

A reasonably skilled pilot can shoot down drones with the jets on-board gun. These use inexpensive $100 shells. Hence the ammunition cost is insignificant compared to anti-air missiles. What remains is the operation cost of the F16. We don't know Ukraine's operating cost for the donated old F16s. It might be $10-20,000/hr. 

Hence a 2h jet mission that takes out 5-10 drones, gives a very low per downed drone cost of $4000. Compare that to the currently least expensive western ground based missile, the IRIS T at about $500,000 per missile. 

Ukraine's and the west's problem is to arrange more donations of used aircraft. 16 used previous generation Swedish Gripen C-D with a claimed even cheaper $5000/hr operating cost will be welcome in 2027, but really, there are thousands of unused older F16s wordwide that could be refurbished and donated.

You don’t mention how Texas (and other states of both colours) has maintained its Republican supermajority, effectively establishing single-party rule: gerrymandering. The state’s metropolitan centres, including Austin, Houston, and Dallas/Fort Worth, are “blue dots” on the state’s map, but they are “cracked” so that their population is effectively disenfranchised. The Supreme Court has said partisan gerrymandering is just fine, even though its (intended) effect is to prevent certain populations from being represented in the state legislature or the House undermining democracy and sidestepping checks and balances.

The one bit of good news is that this year, gerrymandering may not guarantee them so many seats and attempts to supergerrymander even more districts at Trump’s command may backfire. Republicans in Texas and other states had to squeeze even more “reliably Republican” districts out of the same number of voters — voters who, though reliably Republican in the past, are not guaranteed this year. Many are sufficiently unhappy about rising prices, corruption, the war in Iran, etc., that they may decide either to vote for a Democrat, or not to vote.

By giving so many states de facto one-party rule, gerrymandering has disenfranchised populations that support the minority party (making proportional representation a poor joke), contributed to the crisis of hyperpartisanship, and enhanced extremism, since there is not enough competition to keep it in check.

Deck planking (or simply "decking") is horizontal. It has an above and a below but no "behind". Siding, though, is vertical. Siding is exposed to weather on the outside. It protects the rest of the wall from water intrusion. Where siding meets other wall elements that must be exposed (windows and doors, for example), flashing is used to direct any water that has gotten behind siding back to the outside.
